transcript.speech: Out of these 24 jars of jelly, which one would you pick? Well, let me narrow it down for you. Choose
This is part 14 in my Build for Good UX series. And this video actually isn't about jelly or jam, whatever you want to call it.
It is about Hick's Law. The law states that the time that it takes to make a decision increases with the complexity and the number of choices.
And this applies to a lot of things in daily life. Like me asking you to pick from 24 jars versus six.
Or when you're sitting at Cheesecake Factory looking at their 250 item menu compared to going to an In-N-Out where there's basically four options.
And this concept doesn't change when you're thinking about the internet and how to design for a user. Look at Google
versus Yahoo. The web browser will give you one clear action: search. Yahoo has so much going
on, you could call it clutter, but really it's a lot of unnecessary additional choices competing for your attention.
So, instead of showing someone a long form all at once, break it up into several pages.
Studies have shown that if you have over seven fields, multi-page can increase conversion by over 300%.
Instead of this menu where everything is listed out, keep a couple of options and then let people filter in the search results.
And often it's not about limiting what a person can do, it's more about keeping the options manageable.
Netflix does a good job of this where 80% of what you watch comes from recommendations, not what you search.
They have thousands and thousands of movies you can watch, but you don't see them all at once. And the home page is just a few curated rows. And clearly it works.
In the next part, we're going to talk about Progressive Disclosure, so follow for more.

visual_demonstrations.observation: A single long form titled 'Create Account' displaying six visible fields transitions into a multi-step step-by-step UI card titled '1/3 Basic Info' with a progress bar and 'Next Step' button.
visual_demonstrations.before: A white card UI listing 'First Name', 'Last Name', 'Email Address', 'Phone Number', and 'Company Name' fields all at once.
visual_demonstrations.after: A multi-step card displaying '1/3 Basic Info', two input fields ('Full Name', 'Email Address'), and a prominent blue 'Next Step' button.

visual_demonstrations.observation: A mobile ecommerce menu showing 15 individual category links in a vertical list is replaced by a simplified menu showing four top-level category cards ('Women's Clothes', 'Men's Clothes', 'Women's Shoes', 'Men's Shoes') leading to a product grid page with horizontal filter chips.
visual_demonstrations.before: A long vertical menu drawer listing specific items like 'Women's High Heels', 'Women's T-Shirts', 'Men's Sneakers', etc.
visual_demonstrations.after: Top-level category cards transitioning to a product view with horizontal scroll filter tabs ('Dresses', 'Tops', 'T-Shirts', 'Blouses', 'Jeans') outlined in red.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Instead of showing a user a long form all at once, divide it across several pages/steps. For forms with more than seven fields, multi-page structures can increase conversions by over 300%.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Demonstrated visually by converting a long 'Create Account' form with many text inputs into a multi-step card wizard UI showing '1/3 Basic Info' and a 'Next Step' button.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Presenting a long single-page form creates choice overload and decision fatigue.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Split forms containing more than seven fields across multiple pages/steps.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Replace a single scrolling list of fields with step-based wizard cards featuring progress bars and step navigation buttons.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Hick's Law states decision time increases with choice complexity; reducing visible options per screen reduces cognitive load and significantly improves conversion rates.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Web and mobile form design, onboarding flows, and account registration processes with >7 fields.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Instead of exhaustive navigation menus listing every subcategory, show a few top-level categories and allow users to filter on results pages.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Demonstrated by replacing an exhaustive vertical list of 15+ subcategories with 4 main category buttons, followed by horizontal filter chips on the category results page.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Exhaustive menus with dozens of choices overload users during navigation.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Provide broad top-level category options in main menus and defer specific subcategory selection to result-page filters.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Reduce main menu item count and introduce horizontal filter chips on the listings page.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Limits initial choices in accordance with Hick's Law, keeping UI choices manageable without restricting total functionality.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: E-commerce store navigation menus and search UI design.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Google provides one clear primary action (search) on its browser view, whereas Yahoo presents cluttered additional choices competing for user attention.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Side-by-side comparison of Google's single search input page versus Yahoo's home page filled with news cards, ads, and trending widgets.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Too many competing visual widgets and choices distract users from key tasks.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Simplify primary landing interfaces to highlight the single key user action.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Remove peripheral media blocks and secondary links to focus on a prominent search input field.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Reducing choices speeds up decision-making and reduces user effort.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Web homepages, search engines, and portal landing pages.

analyst_interpretation.interpretation: The video uses Hick's Law to argue for chunking information into discrete steps (forms) and progressive disclosure (menus and recommendation carousels).
inferences_not_shown_or_said: The exact source or study behind the '300% conversion increase for >7 fields' statistic is not cited on screen.
